summary.text: At \(n=9\), the product of the first nine primes is \(223092870\), giving \(49770428644836901=29^2\cdot53\cdot1116604864937\). Thus this term is divisible by the square of the nonunit \(29\), so it is not squarefree and the conjunction fails regardless of its infinitude clause.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}p_k,
\]
where \(p_0=2,p_1=3,p_2=5,\ldots\) are the primes in increasing order. Thus the sequence in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=P_n^2+1.
\]
(The empty product gives \(a(0)=2\).) We disprove the assertion that every \(a(n)\) is squarefree by considering \(n=9\).

The first nine primes, with the zero-based indexing used above, are
\[
p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_8=2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_9
 &=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13\cdot17\cdot19\cdot23\\
 &=223092870.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
a(9)=223092870^2+1=49770428644836901.
\]

Now consider the prime \(29\). It is prime because any proper prime divisor of \(29\) would be at most \(\sqrt{29}<6\), hence would have to be one of \(2,3,5\), whereas \(29\) is divisible by none of these. We show that \(29^2=841\) divides \(a(9)\).

One can see this directly from the congruence
\[
223092870=841\cdot265270+800.
\]
Thus
\[
P_9\equiv800\equiv-41\pmod{841}.
\]
Squaring and adding one gives
\[
P_9^2+1\equiv(-41)^2+1=1681+1=1682=2\cdot841\equiv0\pmod{841}.
\]
Therefore
\[
29^2\mid a(9).
\]
For completeness, the exact integer factorization witnessing this divisibility is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(9)
 &=49770428644836901\\
 &=841\cdot59180057841661\\
 &=29^2\cdot53\cdot1116604864937.
\end{aligned}
\]

A positive integer is squarefree precisely when no square of a prime divides it (equivalently, when no integer greater than \(1\) has its square dividing it). Since the square of the prime \(29\) divides \(a(9)\), the number \(a(9)\) is not squarefree. Hence the universal assertion
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad a(n)\text{ is squarefree}
\]
is false.

The conjecture under consideration is the conjunction of this universal squarefreeness assertion and the assertion that the set of indices \(n\) for which \(a(n)\) is prime is infinite. A conjunction can hold only if each of its two conjuncts holds. Its first conjunct already fails at \(n=9\), independently of whether the second conjunct is true or false. Therefore the entire conjunction is false.
